salmonofdoubt.png.title: The Salmon of Doubt
salmonofdoubt.png.author: Douglas Adams
salmonofdoubt.png.summary: A posthumous collection of Douglas Adams's unfinished novel, essays, speeches, and correspondence.
salmonofdoubt.png.thoughts: i'm a big fan of the hitchhiker's guide to the galaxy, and douglas adams' sense of humor in general -- so i'd never pass down a chance to read more of his work. found this at halfpricebooks and it was an immediate cop.

bible.png.title: Holy Bible
bible.png.summary: The New Testament, King James edition.
bible.png.thoughts: some street evangelist in uw's red square offered me his own copy. i was going to decline, but i saw post-it notes sticking out and got curious what the guy chose to highlight. put it right next to "the system of materialism" on my bookshelf because symmetry

systemofmaterialism.png.title: The System of Materialism
systemofmaterialism.png.summary: Three anonymous manuscripts on atheistic metaphysics, clandestinely distributed across 1700s Europe.
systemofmaterialism.png.thoughts: picked this up back in my cynical teenage atheistic phase

makesomethingwonderful.png.title: Make Something Wonderful
makesomethingwonderful.png.author: Steve Jobs Archive
makesomethingwonderful.png.summary: Jobs in his own words, assembled from speeches, interviews, emails, and internal notes across his life and work.
makesomethingwonderful.png.thoughts: beautiful collector's edition, shout out to avi

thethirddoor.png.title: The Third Door
thethirddoor.png.author: Alex Banayan
thethirddoor.png.summary: A college dropout, freshly in pursuit of meaning, tracks down the likes of Bill Gates, Warren Buffett, and Steven Spielberg to learn their shared secret mentality toward success.
thethirddoor.png.thoughts: for how much i quote this book i really should read it lmao

jonathanlivingston.png.title: Jonathan Livingston Seagull
jonathanlivingston.png.author: Richard Bach
jonathanlivingston.png.summary: A short fable about a seagull obsessed with flying for flying's sake.
jonathanlivingston.png.thoughts:
i remember finding this as a kid and thinking it was one of the weirdest stories i'd ever read. all these years later, i agree with myself. why is the seagull teleporting??

cool photos

geb.png.title: Gödel, Escher, Bach
geb.png.author: Douglas R. Hofstadter
geb.png.summary: A sprawling puzzle-box about self-referential loops, overlaps between math/art/music, and how cognition and consciousness emerge from hidden neurological mechanisms.
geb.png.thoughts:
this one honestly didn't need the introduction. you've heard of it, i've heard of it, neither of us have fully read it.

(i promise i will soon)

clockofthelongnow.png.title: The Clock of the Long Now
clockofthelongnow.png.author: Stewart Brand
clockofthelongnow.png.summary: A case for thinking on civilizational timescales, framed around the engineering of a 10,000-year clock; the table of contents itself is enumerated in seconds.
clockofthelongnow.png.thoughts:
i bought this book for a literal dollar at a uw library flash sale, mostly based on the title alone. little did i know that the author was the same guy behind the "whole earth catalog" that steve jobs always used to glaze, not to mention him being a familiar face from the cybernetics world.

brand touches on a lot of ideas, ranging from the need for long-long-term responsibility to the psychological effect of the far future. the most interesting idea to me was "pace layers" -- the idea that civilization is stack of systems operating on radically different timescales depending on the lens: fashion, commerce, infrastructure, nature... i'm curious how it could connect to the multiple temporal hierarchy active predictive coding.

tbh haven't finished this one yet either, i'll write here with my full thoughts once i do

justforfun.png.title: Just for Fun
justforfun.png.author: Linus Torvalds
justforfun.png.summary: Linus's thoughts on his early life, last name, the beginnings of Linux, and the strange satisfactions of building a thing because it is interesting.
justforfun.png.thoughts: linus is a very interesting character. i've always been a mild fan, so when i heard he had a autobiography i bought it immediately. i did not consider that my reading list was already a very long queue. i hope i can get to this soon

dictionary.png.title: The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows
dictionary.png.author: John Koenig
dictionary.png.summary: An invented dictionary for emotions that don't have a name in the English language, complete with proper definitions and etymologies.
dictionary.png.thoughts:
i first came across this project when i was in the eigth grade, and i've been following it religiously ever since. koenig's words and videos had a huge impact on me, and i give him partial credit for the person i am/try to be today.

i'd only ever seen koenig's youtube series (highly recommend, they are works of art) but for my 19th birthday, my girlfriend arisha got me a physical copy of the dictionary. best gift i've ever received.

zen.png.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
zen.png.author: Robert M. Pirsig
zen.png.summary: A strange mix of road trip narration, philosophical argument, ghost story, metaphorical motorcycle maintenance tips, and actual motorcycle maintenance tips.
zen.png.thoughts: really good from what i read but i ended up dropping it after a few chapters. i'll come back to it eventually and leave my thoughts here when i do!

emergence.png.title: Emergence
emergence.png.author: Steven Johnson
emergence.png.summary: An exploration of how complex behavior can arise from simple "dumb" local interactions, from ant colonies and brains to cities and software.
emergence.png.thoughts:
my original exposure to complexity theory was igor's cybernetics symposium in summer 2025. since then i've been kinda obsessed with how lower-level interaction can yield higher-order complexity -- and crucially, how we can nudge emergent qualities toward a desired behavior.

this book was the perfect jump in, offering a compelling introduction to the history (and general vibes) of self-organizing systems. johnson has some witty lines and picked some great examples, even if he does tend to be a little circular. overall strong recommend!
